n: T

- *fifty-five years*: Manasseh's long rule, from 697 to 642 BC was not due to his faithfulness to the Lord, but because the Lord honored his covenant promises (see also {{2 Kings 8:19|2 Kings 8:19}}; {{2 Kings 19:34|19:34}}; {{2 Kings 20:6|20:6}}; {{2 Samuel 7:11-16|2 Samuel 7:11–16}}). External conditions were mostly stable. Although Assyrian kings Esarhaddon (680–669 BC) and Ashurbanipal (668–626 BC) led several military campaigns, they did not target Judah until later in Manasseh’s reign, likely around 650 to 648 BC (see {{2 Chronicles 33:10-13|2 Chronicles 33:10–13}}). Ashurbanipal focused on building projects, religious activities, and the arts, including creating a great library.

- *he did evil*: Manasseh was the most wicked king of Judah. Discussions about his reign highlight his evil religious practices.
B

Manasseh didn’t follow Hezekiah’s example. He did more evil things than any king in Judah before him. He led the people to worship false gods and follow Canaanite practices that God hated. This included sacrificing children.

Manasseh also murdered many people in Jerusalem. Through the prophets, God announced that his people could no longer continue living in their land. They had made the land unclean with their evil deeds. They hadn’t lived as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. So God told them how they would be punished for making the land unclean.

The worst part of the covenant curses would happen to the southern kingdom. Jerusalem and Judah would be destroyed like Samaria and the northern kingdom had been destroyed. Amon was the next king and he followed Manasseh’s example. Josiah ruled after him. Josiah didn’t do evil like Manasseh did. He followed David’s example.

Josiah listened when the Book of the Law was read out loud. This was a copy of the Law of Moses. Josiah’s heart was humble and tender toward God and the law. This pleased God. The prophet Huldah announced that God wouldn’t allow Judah to be destroyed while Josiah was alive.

Josiah led the people to commit again to obeying the Mount Sinai covenant. He got rid of everything that had to do with worshipping false gods. This included altars and high places.

Josiah also led the people in celebrating the Passover Feast. He made sure that the Law of Moses was followed in Judah.
T

Manasseh turned away from his faith by rebuilding local pagan shrines that his father had destroyed ({{2 Kings 18:3|2 Kings 18:3}}). He also encouraged evil religious practices linked to Baal worship and set up an Asherah pole (see {{2 Kings 18:3|2 Kings 18:3}}; {{1 Kings 16:32|1 Kings 16:32}}) and brought back the worship of stars. God had judged the northern kingdom for these sins ({{2 Kings 17:16|2 Kings 17:16}}).
T

- Manasseh's evil actions included taking part in the terrible Molech ceremonies and various forbidden cult and occult practices ({{2 Kings 16:3|2 Kings 16:3}}; see {{Leviticus 18:21|Leviticus 18:21}}). 

- *provoking Him to anger*: God reacted to Manasseh's awful religious practices with fair judgment, just as he did with the northern kingdom ({{2 Kings 17:18-20|2 Kings 17:18–20}}).
T

- The Amorites lived in the land before the Israelites and were known for their wickedness. 

- Manasseh followed the idolatrous practices of the Amorites, just as Ahab did ({{1 Kings 21:26|1 Kings 21:26}}).
T

Given what happened to the northern kingdom ({{2 Kings 17:7-23|2 Kings 17:7–23}}) and Ahab’s family ({{2 Kings 9:24-26|2 Kings 9:24–26}}, {{2 Kings 9:30-37|30–37}}; {{2 Kings 10:1-8|10:1–8}}; {{1 Kings 22:37-38|1 Kings 22:37–38}}), Manasseh should expect God to bring justice to him and the people of Judah.
T

*the remnant*: Those not killed in God's coming judgment would be at the mercy of their captors. This prophecy came true when thousands of Judeans were taken captive during the Babylonian invasion and the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC ({{2 Kings 25:8-21|2 Kings 25:8–21}}; {{2 Chronicles 36:20|2 Chronicles 36:20}}; {{Jeremiah 39:9|Jeremiah 39:9}}; {{Jeremiah 52:15|52:15}}).
T
*innocent blood*: Besides his terrible spiritual sins, Manasseh committed murder. According to Jewish tradition, Manasseh killed many prophets, including Isaiah.
T

*all his accomplishments*: The writer of Chronicles notes that Manasseh was captured by an Assyrian king. This likely happened when King Ashurbanipal was in Babylon, around 650 to 648 BC. This event humbled Manasseh and led to his repentance. After his release, he tried to make spiritual changes, but it was too late in his reign for them to succeed ({{2 Chronicles 33:11-17|2 Chronicles 33:11–17}}).
T

The garden of Uzza is not mentioned elsewhere (but see also {{2 Kings 21:26|2 Kings 21:26}}). Unlike his father Hezekiah, who was buried with honor, Manasseh was not buried in the royal tombs ({{2 Chronicles 32:33|2 Chronicles 32:33}}).
T

- Amon ruled briefly from 642 to 640 BC and continued his father's evil ways. Manasseh's repentance and reforms were too late to influence Amon or the people of Judah. 

- *He abandoned the LORD*: Amon completely rejected his faith (see also {{2 Chronicles 33:23|2 Chronicles 33:23}}).
T
Like his father Manasseh ({{2 Kings 21:17|2 Kings 21:17}}), Amon was not buried in the royal tombs. He was buried in the garden of Uzza instead.
T

- Josiah became the king of Judah in 640 BC. Like Joash ({{2 Kings 11:21|2 Kings 11:21}}), he was still a child when he became king. He was loyal to the Lord, much like David, Asa ({{1 Kings 15:11|1 Kings 15:11}}), and Hezekiah ({{2 Kings 18:3|2 Kings 18:3}}). 

- *did what was right*: Josiah's actions followed the high standards of the law ({{Deuteronomy 17:11|Deuteronomy 17:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:14|28:14}}).
T

- By the eighteenth year of his reign, which was in 621 BC, Josiah had followed the Lord for ten years (see {{2 Chronicles 34:3-7|2 Chronicles 34:3–7}}). 

- Hilkiah, the high priest, came from Zadok's family line ({{1 Chronicles 9:10-11|1 Chronicles 9:10–11}}). Some scholars think this Hilkiah was Jeremiah’s father ({{Jeremiah 1:1|Jeremiah 1:1}}).

- The money was collected in a large chest placed where people could easily access it as they entered the temple (compare {{2 Kings 12:9|2 Kings 12:9}}).
T
Josiah gave Shaphan instructions similar to those Joash gave for repairing the temple during his rule ({{2 Kings 12:10-15|2 Kings 12:10–15}}).
T

The scroll called the Book of the Law might have included all or part of Deuteronomy or even the entire Pentateuch (compare {{Deuteronomy 31:26|Deuteronomy 31:26}}). We do not know how it was lost or where it was found in the temple. Shaphan quickly reported the important discovery and read it to the king.
T

- Like Hezekiah before him ({{2 Kings 19:1|2 Kings 19:1}}), Josiah tore his clothes in deep sorrow for his own spiritual state and that of the people of Judah. 

- *have not obeyed the words of this book*: The part Shaphan read to Josiah reminded him of God's claim on his people, the need to stay faithful to the covenant, and the consequences for unfaithfulness (see {{Deuteronomy 28:1-68|Deuteronomy 28}}). Realizing that Judah had not followed the law, Josiah rightly feared the Lord's great anger.
T

*Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum*: Some suggest Shallum was related to Jeremiah (see {{Jeremiah 32:7-12|Jeremiah 32:7–12}}). Huldah's family ties might have let her serve as a court prophet (see also {{2 Chronicles 34:22-28|2 Chronicles 34:22–28}}).
T

*this is what the LORD says*: Like Miriam ({{Exodus 15:20|Exodus 15:20}}) and Deborah ({{Judges 4:4|Judges 4:4}}), Huldah had the honor of sharing God's message with the people. Huldah confirmed Josiah's fears that God would punish Jerusalem for the people's unfaithfulness and many sins.
T
God praised Josiah for his sorrow and humility after hearing God's word. Although God's judgment was sure, God would delay it until after Josiah's death.
T

Following the instructions in Deuteronomy ({{Deuteronomy 31:10-13|Deuteronomy 31:10–13}}) and the example of Joshua ({{Joshua 8:34-35|Joshua 8:34–35}}), Josiah called all the people to listen to the reading of the entire Book of the Covenant.
T

*the king … made a covenant*: The king … renewed the covenant: God’s people renewed their covenant (their promises with God) at several important times in history (see {{2 Kings 11:12|2 Kings 11:12}}, {{2 Kings 11:17|17}}; {{Joshua 24:1-27|Joshua 24:1–27}}; {{1 Kings 8:1-53|1 Kings 8:1–53}}).
T

- *remove … all the articles*: Josiah removed detestable items related to pagan worship from the temple. 

- *the fields of Kidron*: The fields of the Kidron Valley were close to the Valley of Ben-Hinnom. In that valley, people once carried out ceremonies for the god Molech. These ceremonies involved burning children as sacrifices. Later, the Kidron Valley became a place where ashes and dead bodies were taken ({{Jeremiah 26:23|Jeremiah 26:23}}). 

- Taking the ashes to Bethel, where Jeroboam set up one of his cult altars ({{1 Kings 12:28-29|1 Kings 12:28–29}}), would defile the site forever.
T

Josiah removed the priests who led idol worship. He also destroyed the living places of the cult prostitutes. These practices had been allowed by Manasseh and Amon. They continued the prostitution that came from Canaanite religion (see {{1 Kings 14:24|1 Kings 14:24}}; {{1 Kings 15:12|15:12}}; {{1 Kings 22:46|22:46}}). Shockingly, this was practiced inside the temple itself.
T

The gate of Joshua is not mentioned elsewhere. It might have been used by the city governor. This title refers to a city official in Samaria ({{1 Kings 22:26|1 Kings 22:26}}; {{2 Chronicles 18:25|2 Chronicles 18:25}}) and to Maaseiah in Jerusalem ({{2 Chronicles 34:8|2 Chronicles 34:8}}).
T

- Topheth was an area in the valley of Ben-Hinnom, southwest of the city of David, leading into the Kidron Valley. People once practiced child sacrifice there. 

- Molech is linked to several gods (see {{1 Kings 11:5|1 Kings 11:5}}, {{1 Kings 11:7|7}}, {{1 Kings 11:33|33}}) and is also associated with a sacrifice offered to Baal ({{Jeremiah 7:31-32|Jeremiah 7:31–32}}; {{Jeremiah 19:5-6|19:5–6}}; {{Jeremiah 32:35|32:35}}).
T

- In the ancient Near East, people often used the horse in ceremonies that honored the sun. The Assyrian sun-god Shamash and other gods were shown riding in horse-drawn chariots across the sky. Archaeological findings suggest that a solar cult (worship of the sun) existed in Israel as early as the 800s BC. This practice grew more popular during the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, when the royal court supported it ({{2 Kings 21:3-5|2 Kings 21:3–5}}, {{2 Kings 21:21-22|21–22}}). 

King Josiah tried to end these practices with his reforms. But after his death, the prophet Ezekiel condemned people again for sun worship. He described them as bowing down to the sun in the inner court of the temple ({{Ezekiel 8:16|Ezekiel 8:16}}).

- *an official*: This word *eunuch *(translated *official* in the Berean Standard Bible) does not always mean a man who was physically made a eunuch. It can also mean a high-ranking court official who served the king.
T
*the upper chamber of Ahaz*: People used rooftop altars for star worship ({{Jeremiah 19:13|Jeremiah 19:13}}; {{Zephaniah 1:5|Zephaniah 1:5}}) and Baal rituals ({{Jeremiah 32:29|Jeremiah 32:29}}).
T
Solomon built the pagan shrines because he had many foreign wives ({{1 Kings 11:5|1 Kings 11:5}}, {{1 Kings 11:7|7}}, {{1 Kings 11:33|33}}).
T

Jeroboam built the altar at Bethel to make it easier for Israelites to worship nearby instead of traveling to Jerusalem ({{1 Kings 12:26-31|1 Kings 12:26–31}}). Josiah's destruction of the site followed the law's requirements ({{Deuteronomy 7:5|Deuteronomy 7:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:3|12:3}}) and fulfilled the earlier prophecy by the man of God who had condemned the altar ({{1 Kings 13:1-3|1 Kings 13:1–3}}).
T

*Samaria … high places*: Josiah's religious reforms reached the former northern kingdom (see also {{2 Chronicles 34:6-7|2 Chronicles 34:6–7}}). Josiah's ability to make these changes shows his power and Assyria's decline (see study note on 2 Kings 23:29).
T

- Hezekiah celebrated the Passover with some changes ({{2 Chronicles 30:1-4|2 Chronicles 30:1–4}}, {{2 Chronicles 30:13|13}}, {{2 Chronicles 30:23-27|23–27}}). Josiah's Passover followed the law's strict rules ({{2 Chronicles 35:1-19|2 Chronicles 35:1–19}}). 

- The eighteenth year was when they found the Book of the Law ({{2 Kings 22:3|2 Kings 22:3}}, {{2 Kings 22:8|8}}).
T

Josiah's dedication to the law led to changes in Jerusalem and Judah. He worked hard to remove all bad practices and strictly observed Passover. This made him the greatest king in following the laws of Moses.
T

*I will remove Judah*: Even though Josiah made strong reforms, Manasseh's wickedness was deeply rooted among the people. Josiah could not change their unfaithful hearts, so they would face the consequences for breaking God's covenant ({{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|Deuteronomy 28:15–68}}).
B

When Josiah was king the southern kingdom obeyed God. Yet after he died they didn’t stay faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. They were committed to doing things that went against what God wanted. The kings Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah led the nation to do evil things.

God’s anger at all the evil things his people did was very strong. So God brought judgement against the southern kingdom. Nebuchadnezzar and the army of Babylon were God’s tool. God used them to bring the covenant curses on Judah. This happened in 587 and 586 BC.

The Babylonians broke down the wall around Jerusalem. They burnt the king’s palace and many important buildings. They carried away the objects used to worship God in the temple. And they completely destroyed the temple. God had told Solomon that this would happen if Israel’s kings worshipped false gods (1 Kings 9:6­–9).

The Babylonians forced many people in Judah and Jerusalem to leave their land. They were taken to live in Babylon. This was called the exile of the southern kingdom. Those who were left in Judah didn’t live in peace and rest. There was fighting over who would be the leader. Many people ran away to live in Egypt.

Jehoiachin was the only king from David’s family line who hadn’t died or been killed. He was in prison in Babylon until a ruler after Nebuchadnezzar set him free.
T
The end of Josiah's reign includes a historical note about his death by Pharaoh Neco (see also {{2 Chronicles 35:20-25|2 Chronicles 35:20–25}}).
T

In 609 BC, Pharaoh Neco was heading to the Euphrates River to assist the Assyrian king against the Babylonians at Haran. Josiah confronted him at Megiddo. 

After Assyrian king Ashurbanipal died in 626 BC, Assyrian cities began falling to Nabopolassar, the king of the growing Neo-Babylonian empire. 

Nabopolassar captured Nineveh, Assyria's capital, in 612 BC. The Assyrian forces retreated to Haran, where the Babylonians defeated them in 609 BC. 

Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon later defeated the remaining Assyrians at Carchemish in 605 BC, the same year he first invaded Judah (see {{2 Kings 24:1|2 Kings 24:1}}).
T
The writer of Chronicles tells how Josiah was greatly honored after his death ({{2 Chronicles 35:24-25|2 Chronicles 35:24–25}}).
T

- Jehoahaz was originally named Shallum at birth (see study note on 1 Chronicles 3:15). His throne name, Jehoahaz, has been found on seals from the 600s BC. He became king at twenty-three, while his brother Jehoiakim was twenty-five ({{2 Kings 23:36|2 Kings 23:36}}). There is no explanation for why the younger brother became king. 

- Jehoahaz reigned for three months in 609 BC, possibly during the time when Pharaoh Neco was trying to help the Assyrians ({{2 Kings 23:29|2 Kings 23:29}}).
T

*he did evil in the sight of the LORD*: The deep-rooted evil and turning away from faith of the time appeared even in Josiah’s sons ({{2 Kings 23:32|2 Kings 23:32}}, {{2 Kings 23:37|37}}; {{2 Kings 24:9|24:9}}, {{2 Kings 24:19|19}}). The Lord planned to judge Judah ({{2 Kings 23:26-27|2 Kings 23:26–27}}), and this decision was justified and would soon happen.
T
Riblah was a strong administrative center in Aramean territory, located about sixty miles northeast of Damascus.
T
*Eliakim … Jehoiakim*: Neco followed the Assyrian tradition of demanding a loyalty oath and giving a new name to the local leader.
T
Jehoiakim, Jehoahaz’s older brother (see {{2 Kings 23:31|2 Kings 23:31}}), ruled for eleven years from 609 to 598 BC.
T

*did evil*: The book of Jeremiah describes Jehoiakim as completely unfaithful (see {{Jeremiah 22:13-23|Jeremiah 22:13–23}}; {{Jeremiah 25:1-14|25:1–14}}; {{Jeremiah 26:20-23|26:20–23}}; {{Jeremiah 36:1-32|36:1–32}}).
T

In 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar led forces that defeated the last Assyrian army and an Egyptian group at Carchemish (see {{Jeremiah 46:2|Jeremiah 46:2}}). While he was campaigning in the west, his father, Nabopolassar, died. 

Nebuchadnezzar returned home to become king as Nebuchadnezzar II from 605 to 562 BC. When he rejoined his troops, they easily advanced down the Mediterranean coast. During this campaign, he invaded Judah, taking much treasure and many captives to Babylon, including Daniel and his three friends ({{Daniel 1:1-7|Daniel 1:1–7}}). Jehoiakim became a vassal to Nebuchadnezzar and paid him tribute for three years. 

When Pharaoh Neco defeated the Babylonians at the Egyptian border in 601 BC, Jehoiakim rebelled, hoping to gain independence.
T

Nebuchadnezzar II attacked Judah at least three times, in 605 BC, 597 BC, and 586 BC.

He took treasures from Jerusalem and captured people to bring to Babylon (see {{2 Kings 24:1|2 Kings 24:1}}, {{2 Kings 24:10-17|10–17}}; {{2 Kings 25:1-21|25:1–21}}).
T
Nebuchadnezzar waited from 601 to 598 BC while strengthening his control over the west. He sent raiders to attack Judah.
T
*at the LORD’s command*: Judah's main issue was its stubborn spiritual unfaithfulness. Even with Josiah's reforms, Manasseh's sins deeply affected Judah, making divine judgment unavoidable.
T
*innocent blood*: Tradition says that Manasseh killed the prophet Isaiah by cutting him in half (see {{Hebrews 11:37|Hebrews 11:37}}).
T

Jehoiakim died in 598 BC, likely during Nebuchadnezzar’s second attack on Jerusalem. Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar executed Jehoiakim (see Josephus, *Antiquities* 10.6.3; compare {{Jeremiah 22:18-19|Jeremiah 22:18–19}}; {{Jeremiah 36:30-31|36:30–31}}).
T

- The king of Egypt stayed in his country because Nebuchadnezzar was too powerful. Judah's hope for help from Egypt was useless (see {{Jeremiah 2:36|Jeremiah 2:36}}; {{Jeremiah 46:2-12|46:2–12}}; {{Ezekiel 29:6|Ezekiel 29:6}}, {{Ezekiel 29:16|16}}). 

- The Brook of Egypt is thought to be either the Wadi el-Arish near the Nile delta or Nahal Besor, south of Gaza.
T

- Jehoiachin became king in 597 BC. 

- He ruled in Jerusalem for three months (see {{Jeremiah 22:28-30|Jeremiah 22:28–30}}).
T

- Jehoiachin gave up when Nebuchadnezzar's powerful army approached. See study note on 2 Chronicles 36:9–10. 

- Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year as king was 597 BC.
T

- *As the LORD had declared*: See {{2 Kings 20:16-17|2 Chronicles 20:16–17}}. A greater divine judgment was still to come ({{2 Kings 21:12-15|2 Kings 21:12–15}}; {{2 Kings 22:15-20|22:15–20}}; {{2 Kings 23:26-27|23:26–27}}). 

- *all the treasures*: During his earlier attack on Jerusalem in 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar took some of the temple treasures as loot ({{2 Chronicles 36:7|2 Chronicles 36:7}}; {{Daniel 1:2|Daniel 1:2}}). He now took all the treasures. Anything left behind was taken during his final attack on Jerusalem in 586 BC ({{2 Kings 25:15|2 Kings 25:15}}).
T

- Along with Jehoiachin, the prophet Ezekiel was also taken into captivity ({{Ezekiel 1:1|Ezekiel 1:1}}). The book of Ezekiel dates events in his life based on the years since Jehoiachin's capture. 

- The 10,000 people taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar likely included: 

- 7,000 troops,

- 1,000 craftsmen and artisans, and

- several administrative officials and leading citizens of Jerusalem.

The number *10,000* is probably an estimate (see also {{Jeremiah 52:28|Jeremiah 52:28}}).
T

- Like the three kings before him, Mattaniah was given a throne name. His throne name was Zedekiah. 

- *Jehoiachin’s uncle*: See {{1 Chronicles 3:15-16|1 Chronicles 3:15–16}}.
T

- Zedekiah ruled Jerusalem for eleven years, from 597 to 586 BC, and was as evil as Jehoiakim ({{2 Kings 23:36-37|2 Kings 23:36–37}}). The Lord was punishing Jerusalem and Judah for their sins (see {{2 Kings 17:19|2 Kings 17:19}}; {{2 Kings 20:16-17|20:16–17}}; {{2 Kings 21:12-15|21:12–15}}; {{2 Kings 22:15-20|22:15–20}}; {{2 Kings 23:26-27|23:26–27}}). 

- *Zedekiah also rebelled*: His rebellion might have been part of an anti-Babylonian alliance led by Pharaoh Apries of Egypt. When Apries became king around 589 BC, he wanted to restore Egypt's former glory. Zedekiah seemed to trust him (compare {{Ezekiel 17:15-18|Ezekiel 17:15–18}}). However, like earlier kings ({{2 Kings 17:4|2 Kings 17:4}}; {{2 Kings 24:1-3|24:1–3}}), Zedekiah found that Egypt offered little help (compare {{2 Kings 18:20-21|2 Kings 18:20–21}}; {{Jeremiah 37:3-10|Jeremiah 37:3–10}}; {{Ezekiel 29:6-7|Ezekiel 29:6–7}}).
T

Siege ramps were common in ancient Near Eastern warfare. Attackers built a *siege wall* (tall dirt ramps and towers) to gain a better position (see {{Jeremiah 52:14|Jeremiah 52:14}}; {{Ezekiel 21:22|Ezekiel 21:22}}).
T

The Babylonians used battering rams ({{Ezekiel 4:2|Ezekiel 4:2}}) to break a part of Jerusalem's wall and enter the city. At nightfall, King Zedekiah and the remaining troops escaped through the gate at the southeastern corner of the city into the Kidron Valley, trying to reach the Jordan Valley.
T
Riblah, once an Assyrian administrative center, was Nebuchadnezzar’s battle headquarters. It also served the Egyptians ({{2 Kings 23:33|2 Kings 23:33}}).
T

- *they put out his eyes*: In the ancient Near East, rebellious leaders were often blinded. Zedekiah's blinding was especially cruel because his last sight was his sons being killed. 

- True to the prophecy, Zedekiah was captured and died in captivity ({{Jeremiah 32:4-5|Jeremiah 32:4–5}}; {{Jeremiah 34:3|34:3}}; {{Jeremiah 52:11|52:11}}; {{Ezekiel 12:11-14|Ezekiel 12:11–14}}).
T
Nebuzaradan is known from one of Nebuchadnezzar's writings as a high-ranking official.
T
*every significant building*: The Babylonians destroyed important religious and government buildings to prevent further rebellion. They also tore down the city's walls, leaving Jerusalem defenseless.
T

- The Babylonians exiled most of the population, including some who willingly joined them ({{Jeremiah 39:9|Jeremiah 39:9}}; {{Jeremiah 52:15|52:15}}). 

- They left the poorest people behind because they were unlikely to cause trouble and could work the vineyards and fields.
T

The Babylonians dismantled the temple furnishings made by Huram of Tyre and other bronze items (see {{1 Kings 7:13-50|1 Kings 7:13–50}}) for their own use. Transporting these valuable items to Babylon was a major task. They took everything valuable (see also {{Jeremiah 52:17-23|Jeremiah 52:17–23}}).
T

The bronze capital (the decorated top part of the pillar) was 3 cubits high (about 1.4 meters or 4.5 feet). Some ancient copies read 5 cubits (about 2.3 meters or 7.5 feet). This larger number may describe the entire capital, while the Hebrew text may describe only the decorative network of bronze pomegranates (compare {{1 Kings 7:17-18|1 Kings 7:17–18}}).
T

- Instead of deporting important citizens and officials like during the Babylonian invasion of 597 BC ({{2 Kings 24:14|2 Kings 24:14}}), Nebuchadnezzar executed these leaders. He even had religious leaders killed. 

- Seraiah, the high priest, was killed. But his son Jehozadak was exiled ({{1 Chronicles 6:15|1 Chronicles 6:15}}). This allowed the priestly line to continue in captivity and later return to Jerusalem, starting in 538 BC ({{Ezra 1:1-2:20|Ezra 1:1–2:20}}).
T

The people of Judah were exiled from their land. Like the northern kingdom before them, Judah was exiled as punishment for breaking their covenant. A small group later returned to the promised land in 538 BC ({{2 Chronicles 36:22-23|2 Chronicles 36:22–23}}; {{Ezra 1:1-2:20|Ezra 1:1–2:20}}; see also {{2 Chronicles 36:15-21|2 Chronicles 36:15–21}}; {{Jeremiah 25:11|Jeremiah 25:11}}; {{Jeremiah 29:10|29:10}}; {{Daniel 9:2|Daniel 9:2}}).
T

Gedaliah's father, Ahikam, and grandfather, Shaphan, were trusted officials when Josiah was king ({{2 Kings 22:3|2 Kings 22:3}}, {{2 Kings 22:12|12}}). Ahikam supported Jeremiah during Jehoiakim's reign ({{Jeremiah 26:24|Jeremiah 26:24}}).
T

Two short sections describe what happened next. The first explains how the land was reorganized ({{2 Kings 25:22-26|2 Kings 25:22–26}}). The second tells how King Jehoiachin was later treated kindly ({{2 Kings 25:27-30|2 Kings 25:27–30}}).
T

- Gedaliah's family had experience in civic matters, so people initially accepted his role as governor (see also {{Jeremiah 40:1-12|Jeremiah 40:1–12}}). A seal impression found at Lachish shows Gedaliah's importance as the officer "over the house" (see study note on 1 Kings 4:6). 

- The prophet Jeremiah, along with army commanders, went to Mizpah to support Gedaliah ({{Jeremiah 40:6|Jeremiah 40:6}}). This Mizpah was a border town in Benjamin and was known in Israelite history as a place for religious gatherings ({{1 Samuel 7:5-6|1 Samuel 7:5–6}}). 

- The men mentioned here held significant positions. Ishmael came from a royal family ({{2 Kings 25:25|2 Kings 25:25}}; {{Jeremiah 36:12|Jeremiah 36:12}}). Johanan was a loyal supporter of Gedaliah ({{Jeremiah 40:13-16|Jeremiah 40:13–16}}). The name Jezaniah appears on items found during excavations at Tell-en-Nasbeh.
T

Gedaliah was warned that Ishmael planned to kill him, but he did not believe it ({{Jeremiah 40:13-16|Jeremiah 40:13–16}}). His trust led to his death. Ishmael also killed many Judeans and Babylonians, took many captives, and escaped to Ammon ({{Jeremiah 41:4-15|Jeremiah 41:4–15}}).
T
All the people of Judah, led by Johanan, fled in fear to Egypt. They did this even though the prophet Jeremiah had warned them not to go (see {{Jeremiah 42:1-43:7|Jeremiah 42:1–43:7}}).
T

- Evil-merodach (Babylonian, *Amel-marduk*, meaning "man of Marduk") took over after Nebuchadnezzar II died and ruled briefly from 561 to 560 BC. 

- *he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin*: Babylonian records detail the food Jehoiachin received in prison. The mention of Jehoiachin living comfortably might suggest hope that God would protect and bring back a repentant people to their land (see {{1 Kings 8:46-53|1 Kings 8:46–53}}; {{Isaiah 35:8-10|Isaiah 35:8–10}}; {{Isaiah 51:11|51:11}}; {{Jeremiah 29:10-14|Jeremiah 29:10–14}}; {{Zephaniah 3:20|Zephaniah 3:20}}).
